audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor combines biology, medicine and engineering to study ways to repair or regenerate tissues.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The 2026–2027 example uses Maastricht’s clinical design project. The UCR plan combines biomedical science with data analysis, engineering foundations and innovation.

cellNotes.text: Both study the molecular basis of life. UCR focuses on proteins, metabolism and biochemical techniques. Maastricht also uses chemistry and cell biology to introduce regenerative medicine.
Both develop cell biology, including cell fate and stem cells. Maastricht extends this to cell sourcing, manufacture and cell–material constructs.
Both develop molecular laboratory skills. Maastricht also integrates lab practice across its first-year courses.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the first-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Maastricht continues lab training in cell culture, assays and materials. UCR develops related laboratory foundations in its life science lab.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the second-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Both study organ function and physiology. Maastricht combines physiology with anatomy and immunology in the same course.
Both examine immune responses relevant to regenerative treatments. Maastricht also studies therapies and devices, including implants and cell-based treatments.
Both study tissue repair and regeneration. Maastricht concentrates on the regenerative capacity of different tissues and the factors that limit it.
Maastricht introduces regenerative medicine and its applications in society. UCR covers related biology and general ethics across separate courses.
Both develop quantitative and physical foundations. UCR includes mechanics and material properties in sustainability contexts. Maastricht also teaches engineering tools for biomechanics.
UCR studies material properties and characterisation in sustainability. Maastricht focuses on biomaterials and their interaction with cells.
Maastricht teaches specialist methods such as microfabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication.
Both use programming to explore and analyse data. Maastricht’s course combines R scripting and statistics in regenerative-medicine examples.
Both develop data-driven models. Maastricht combines these with differential equations and examples from biological systems.
Both develop and test product concepts in teams. Maastricht uses a clinical regeneration problem. UCR uses consumer products.
Both explore how ideas become marketable products. Maastricht focuses on the value of regenerative-medicine research. UCR teaches general venture design and validation.
Maastricht introduces the design process through interviews, journal clubs, visits and a project pitch.
Both develop academic, communication and reflective skills. Maastricht continues its academic development sequence throughout the year.
Maastricht continues its academic development sequence and prepares students for their minor and graduation project.
Students complete a 30 EC minor. Choices can include courses at Maastricht or another university, with approval where required.
Maastricht’s 30 EC graduation project combines an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled plan.

notes.text: Both plans study biochemistry, cell biology, physiology and data analysis. Maastricht adds specialist work in cell manufacture, biomaterials, gene and cell therapies, microfabrication and clinical design. UCR combines biomedical science with related engineering foundations and product design.

Maastricht combines courses with continuing lab, design and academic development work. In the final year, students take a 30 EC minor and complete a 30 EC graduation project. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENENTR111.name: Consumer Product Design
BENENTR111.text: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.

source.reviewNote: CP089: reviewed the unchanged official description against current course content. The existing text supports the stated scope.

BENENTR311.name: Market Research
BENENTR311.text: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

source.reviewNote: Compared the retained modal with the revised official description. The revision adds promotional wording without changing the substantive account of planning, conducting and analysing market research; the existing concise text remains faithful.

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.text: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.text: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

DISDATA211.text: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.text: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

ENSGATE101.name: Sustainability Essentials I
ENSGATE101.text: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

ENSGATE201.name: Sustainability Essentials II
ENSGATE201.text: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

HCBBIOM211.name: Functional Anatomy
HCBBIOM211.text: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Medical images, anatomical drawing, human-specimen material and guided practicals develop spatial reasoning, including observation in a dissection room. Historical, ethical and societal questions accompany these academic learning activities, which do not provide clinical qualification.

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.text: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.

HCBBIOM312.name: Infection & Immunity
HCBBIOM312.text: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.

HCBBIOM313.name: Mechanisms of Disease
HCBBIOM313.text: Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. Students connect anatomy and physiology with symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Clinical cases and an imaginary-disease assignment develop coherent pathophysiological explanations.

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.text: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Topics include biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, metabolism, cell division, heredity, gene expression and biotechnology. Students analyse scientific experiments and papers through teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium, with additional topics selected with the class.

HCBLIFE211.text: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
